stem_html:
\(\dfrac{2x+5}{3}-\dfrac{x-1}{4}=\dfrac{x+9}{6}\)

What is the solution to the given equation?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The minus sign in front of a fraction. It applies to both terms of the numerator, and the second one is where it usually gets dropped.
  • Clearing denominators unevenly. The least common multiple has to multiply every term, including the one that already has the largest denominator.
  • Losing the sign at the very end. The arithmetic is right and the answer is negative.

Why A is right Multiplying every term by 12 gives \(4(2x+5)-3(x-1)=2(x+9)\), so \(8x+20-3x+3=2x+18\), \(5x+23=2x+18\) and \(x=-\dfrac{5}{3}\).

Why B is wrong This is what comes out if the minus sign in front of the second fraction is distributed to \(x\) but not to \(-1\): \(8x+20-3x-3=2x+18\) gives \(x=\dfrac{1}{3}\).

Why C is wrong Multiplying the left side by 12 but the right side by 6, so that \(x+9\) becomes \(2x+9\), leaves \(5x+23=2x+9\) and \(x=-\dfrac{14}{3}\). Every term has to be multiplied by the same number.

Why D is wrong This is the solution with its sign reversed, which is what a student gets by writing \(3x=5\) instead of \(3x=-5\) at the last step.

stem_html: The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x)=mx+b\), where \(m\) and \(b\) are constants. If \(f(3)=11\) and \(f(-1)=-9\), what is the value of \(f(0)\)?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Slope reported as the answer. The work is finished one step before the question is.
  • Two negatives in the slope formula. \(3-(-1)\) is 4, not 2.
  • A given value that looks like a result. \(-9\) is on the page already.

Why A is right The slope is \(\dfrac{11-(-9)}{3-(-1)}=\dfrac{20}{4}=5\), so \(11=5(3)+b\) and \(b=-4\). Since \(f(0)=b\), the value is \(-4\).

Why B is wrong 5 is the slope, not the value at 0. Reporting \(m\) when the question asks for \(f(0)\) is the single most common way to lose this question.

Why C is wrong Using \(-9=5(-1)+b\) but writing \(-9=-5-b\) gives \(b=-4\) with the wrong sign attached, and \(1\) is what the slip produces when the error is made in the other equation.

Why D is wrong \(-9\) is \(f(-1)\), a value the question supplies. It is the output at \(x=-1\), not at \(x=0\).

skill: Systems of two linear equations in two variables
stem_html:
\(\begin{aligned} 2x+3y &= 13 \\ 4x-y &= 5 \end{aligned}\)

If \((x,y)\) is the solution to the given system, what is the value of \(x-y\)?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The question asks for a combination, not a variable. Both \(x\) and \(y\) appear among the choices.
  • Order of subtraction. \(x-y\) and \(y-x\) differ only by a sign, and both are offered.
  • A number lifted from the system. Choices built out of the givens are there to catch a guess.

Why A is right The second equation gives \(y=4x-5\). Substituting, \(2x+3(4x-5)=13\), so \(14x=28\) and \(x=2\); then \(y=3\). Therefore \(x-y=2-3=-1\).

Why B is wrong \(1\) is \(y-x\). The subtraction is the last operation in the problem and the one most often performed in the wrong order.

Why C is wrong \(2\) is the value of \(x\). The system has been solved correctly and the final question has not been answered.

Why D is wrong \(5\) is the constant on the right of the second equation. It is on the page and it is not a value of anything the question asks for.

skill: Linear inequalities in one or two variables
stem_html: A shipping crate must hold at least 40 items. Each small item weighs 3 kg and each large item weighs 8 kg, and the loaded crate may not exceed 260 kg. If \(s\) is the number of small items and \(\ell\) is the number of large items, which system of inequalities represents these constraints?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “At least” and “no more than” in one sentence. The two inequalities point in opposite directions.
  • Which number counts and which number weighs. 40 belongs to the count constraint and 260 to the mass constraint.
  • Coefficient attachment. 3 goes with small and 8 with large.

Why A is right “At least 40 items” counts items, so \(s+\ell\ge 40\). “May not exceed 260 kg” weighs them, so \(3s+8\ell\le 260\).

Why B is wrong Both inequality signs are reversed. This describes a crate holding at most 40 items and weighing at least 260 kg, which is the opposite of both constraints.

Why C is wrong The two quantities are swapped: this counts kilograms against 40 and items against 260. The 40 is a count and the 260 is a mass.

Why D is wrong The weights are attached to the wrong variables. A small item weighs 3 kg, so 3 must multiply \(s\).

stem_html: Line \(k\) passes through \((-2,7)\) and is perpendicular to the line \(4x-6y=15\). What is the slope of line \(k\)?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Negative reciprocal is two operations. Three of the choices perform one of them.
  • The point is never needed. \((-2,7)\) fixes the line's position and has no effect on its slope.
  • Solving for \(y\) with a negative coefficient. Dividing \(-6y\) flips both signs on the right.

Why A is right Rewriting \(4x-6y=15\) as \(y=\dfrac{2}{3}x-\dfrac{5}{2}\) gives slope \(\dfrac{2}{3}\). The perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal, \(-\dfrac{3}{2}\).

Why B is wrong \(\dfrac{2}{3}\) is the slope of the given line, which is the slope of a parallel line rather than a perpendicular one.

Why C is wrong \(-\dfrac{2}{3}\) negates the slope without taking the reciprocal. Negating alone produces a reflection, not a perpendicular.

Why D is wrong \(\dfrac{3}{2}\) takes the reciprocal without negating, so the two lines would meet at an angle that is not a right angle.

stem_html: A tank is being drained. The volume \(V\), in litres, remaining after \(t\) minutes is given by \(V(t)=480-16t\). To the nearest whole minute, how long after draining begins is the tank three-quarters empty?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Empty against full. Three-quarters empty leaves one quarter, and the complement is the number to put in the equation.
  • Rounding at the right moment. \(22.5\) rounds to 23, and rounding \(V\) instead of \(t\) changes the answer.
  • Landmarks of the model. Empty at 30 and half at 15 are both easy to compute and neither is asked for.

Why A is right Three-quarters empty means one quarter remains, so \(V=120\). Then \(480-16t=120\), \(16t=360\) and \(t=22.5\), which rounds to 23.

Why B is wrong \(t=7.5\), rounded to 8, is when the tank is three-quarters full: \(V=360\). The word “empty” is what separates the two.

Why C is wrong \(t=30\) is when the tank is completely empty, since \(480-16(30)=0\). That is four quarters gone, not three.

Why D is wrong \(t=15\) is the half-way point, \(V=240\). Half is the number reached by dividing 30 by 2 rather than by reading the fraction in the question.

stem_html: In the equation \(a(x+4)-3x=2(x-6)+c\), \(a\) and \(c\) are constants. If the equation has no solution, what is the value of \(a\)?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • No solution and infinitely many solutions share a condition. Both need the \(x\)-coefficients equal; only the constants tell them apart, and this question never needs \(c\).
  • Distributing \(a\) over \(x+4\). The \(4a\) is a constant and does not affect the coefficient condition.
  • Numbers already in the equation. 2 and 3 are both on the page.

Why A is right Expanding gives \((a-3)x+4a=2x-12+c\). An equation with no solution has matching \(x\)-coefficients and different constants, so \(a-3=2\) and \(a=5\).

Why B is wrong 2 is the coefficient of \(x\) on the right. The condition is that \(a-3\) equals it, not that \(a\) does.

Why C is wrong \(-1\) comes from \(a-3=2\) solved as \(a=2-3\). The 3 moves to the other side by addition, not subtraction.

Why D is wrong 3 is the coefficient being subtracted on the left. It appears in the equation and is not the value that makes the coefficients match.

stem_html:
\(\sqrt{2x+11}=x+4\)

What is the sum of all solutions to the given equation?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Squaring can invent a root. Both candidates have to be substituted back into the original equation.
  • “Sum of all solutions” sounds like a job for \(-b/a\). That shortcut sums the roots of the squared equation, including the one that is not a solution.
  • A square root is never negative, so any \(x\) making \(x+4<0\) fails immediately.

Why A is right Squaring gives \(2x+11=x^{2}+8x+16\), so \(x^{2}+6x+5=0\) and \(x=-1\) or \(x=-5\). Checking, \(x=-5\) gives \(\sqrt{1}=1\) on the left and \(-1\) on the right, so it is extraneous. Only \(x=-1\) survives, and the sum of all solutions is \(-1\).

Why B is wrong \(-8\) is the coefficient of \(x\) in the expanded square with its sign kept, and it is also what a student reports after mis-summing the two roots. The roots sum to \(-6\) before the check, not \(-8\).

Why C is wrong \(-7\) is a mis-addition of the two roots. Even the correct sum of both roots, \(-6\), would be wrong here, because one of them does not satisfy the original equation.

Why D is wrong 5 is the constant term of \(x^{2}+6x+5\), which is the product of the roots rather than a solution or a sum of solutions.

stem_html: The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x)=-2(x-3)^{2}+18\). What is the maximum value of \(f\), and at what value of \(x\) does it occur?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "The maximum is 18, at \\(x=3\\)."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "The maximum is 3, at \\(x=18\\).", "trap": "solved-wrong-quantity"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "The maximum is 18, at \\(x=-3\\).", "trap": "sign-flip"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "There is no maximum; \\(f\\) increases without bound.", "trap": "sign-flip"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The sign inside the parentheses. \((x-3)\) puts the vertex at \(+3\).
  • Maximum value against the input that produces it. Both numbers are in the expression, and the choices offer them in both orders.
  • The leading coefficient decides max or min, and it is the one part of the vertex form that is easy to read past.

Why A is right In vertex form \(a(x-h)^{2}+k\) the vertex is \((h,k)\), and \(a=-2<0\) opens the parabola downward, so \(k=18\) is a maximum reached at \(h=3\).

Why B is wrong This swaps the coordinates of the vertex. The value of the function is 18 and the input is 3, not the other way round.

Why C is wrong The sign of \(h\) comes from \((x-h)\), so \((x-3)^{2}\) has \(h=3\). Reading it as \(-3\) reflects the vertex across the \(y\)-axis.

Why D is wrong A parabola with a negative leading coefficient opens downward and is bounded above. Increasing without bound would require \(a>0\), and then there would be a minimum instead.

stem_html: Which expression is equivalent to \(\dfrac{x^{2}-9}{x^{2}+x-12}\) for all \(x\) at which both expressions are defined?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Cancelling terms instead of factors. \(x^{2}\) over \(x^{2}\) is not 1 when either is part of a sum.
  • Sign of the second factor. The middle coefficient \(+1\) fixes it.
  • Which factor is common. Both quadratics contain \((x-3)\); neither contains \((x-4)\).

Why A is right The numerator factors as \((x-3)(x+3)\) and the denominator as \((x-3)(x+4)\). Cancelling the common \((x-3)\) leaves \(\dfrac{x+3}{x+4}\).

Why B is wrong This cancels \((x+3)\) from the numerator against a factor the denominator does not have. \(x^{2}+x-12\) factors into \((x-3)(x+4)\), so \((x+3)\) is not available to cancel.

Why C is wrong This cancels the \(x^{2}\) terms and then the \(x\), which is not a legal operation on a sum. Only common factors of the whole numerator and denominator may be cancelled.

Why D is wrong The denominator's remaining factor is \((x+4)\), not \((x-4)\). Factoring \(-12\) as \((-3)(4)\) requires the signs \(-3\) and \(+4\) to sum to \(+1\).

stem_html:
\(2x^{2}+7x-15=0\)

If \(r\) and \(s\) are the solutions to the given equation and \(r>s\), what is the value of \(r-s\)?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Sum and product are the memorised relations, and the question asks for neither.
  • Subtracting a negative. \(\dfrac{3}{2}-(-5)\) adds.
  • Which root is larger. \(r>s\) fixes the order of the subtraction.

Why A is right Factoring gives \((2x-3)(x+5)=0\), so \(x=\dfrac{3}{2}\) or \(x=-5\). With \(r=\dfrac{3}{2}\) and \(s=-5\), \(r-s=\dfrac{3}{2}+5=\dfrac{13}{2}\).

Why B is wrong \(-\dfrac{7}{2}\) is the sum of the roots, \(-\dfrac{b}{a}\). The question asks for their difference.

Why C is wrong \(\dfrac{7}{2}\) is the sum of the roots with its sign dropped, which is what comes of writing \(\dfrac{b}{a}\) instead of \(-\dfrac{b}{a}\).

Why D is wrong \(\dfrac{11}{2}\) is \(5-\dfrac{3}{2}\) rather than \(\dfrac{3}{2}-(-5)\). Subtracting in the wrong order and then correcting the sign by hand loses the \(+5\).

stem_html: The population of a bacterial culture doubles every 90 minutes. If the culture contains 4,000 cells at 9:00 a.m., which function gives the number of cells \(P(t)\) after \(t\) hours?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The exponent is time divided by the doubling period, and both quantities have to be in the same unit.
  • Minutes on the page, hours in the question. The 90 has to be converted before it is used.
  • Dividing by a fraction. \(t/1.5\) is \(2t/3\), not \(3t/2\).

Why A is right Ninety minutes is \(1.5\) hours, so the number of doublings in \(t\) hours is \(\dfrac{t}{1.5}=\dfrac{2t}{3}\).

Why B is wrong This multiplies by 90 instead of dividing, and it also mixes units: it would give 90 doublings in a single hour.

Why C is wrong Dividing \(t\) by 90 treats \(t\) as a number of minutes, but the question defines \(t\) in hours.

Why D is wrong \(\dfrac{3t}{2}\) is \(t\) divided by \(\dfrac{2}{3}\), the reciprocal of the doubling time. It gives one doubling every 40 minutes.

stem_html: The expression \(\dfrac{6x^{2}+13x-5}{3x-1}\) is equivalent to which of the following for \(x\neq\dfrac{1}{3}\)?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Check the constant term. The product of the two constants must be \(-5\), which settles the signs immediately.
  • Check the leading term. \(3x\) times what gives \(6x^{2}\).
  • Assuming a remainder. Long division is fine, and it ends cleanly.

Why A is right \(6x^{2}+13x-5\) factors as \((3x-1)(2x+5)\), and cancelling \((3x-1)\) leaves \(2x+5\). Checking: \((3x-1)(2x+5)=6x^{2}+15x-2x-5=6x^{2}+13x-5\).

Why B is wrong \((3x-1)(2x-5)=6x^{2}-17x+5\), which is not the numerator. The constant term alone rules it out: \((-1)(-5)=+5\), not \(-5\).

Why C is wrong \((3x-1)(3x+5)=9x^{2}+12x-5\). The leading coefficient has to be 6, so the second factor must begin with \(2x\).

Why D is wrong There is no remainder here; the division comes out exactly. A remainder term is added by a student who divides without noticing the numerator factors.

stem_html: The graph of \(y=f(x)\) has \(x\)-intercepts at \(x=-4\) and \(x=2\) and passes through \((0,-16)\). If \(f\) is quadratic, what is the value of \(f(3)\)?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Forgetting the leading coefficient. The intercepts fix the shape and the extra point fixes the scale.
  • Sign of the product at \(x=3\). Both factors are positive there.
  • A given value among the choices. \(-16\) is already on the page.

Why A is right Write \(f(x)=a(x+4)(x-2)\). Then \(f(0)=a(4)(-2)=-8a\), and \(-8a=-16\) gives \(a=2\). So \(f(3)=2(3+4)(3-2)=2\cdot 7\cdot 1=14\).

Why B is wrong \(-14\) keeps the negative sign of \(f(0)\) even though both factors are positive at \(x=3\). A parabola opening upward is above the axis to the right of its larger root.

Why C is wrong 7 is \((3+4)(3-2)\) with \(a\) left out. Solving for \(a\) is the step the point \((0,-16)\) exists to supply.

Why D is wrong \(-16\) is \(f(0)\), a value the question provides. It is the output at \(x=0\), not at \(x=3\).

stem_html: A jacket's price is reduced by 30 percent. The reduced price is then increased by 30 percent. The final price is what percent of the original price?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Equal percentages, unequal amounts. The second percentage is taken of a smaller number.
  • The answer is below 100 whichever order the changes come in, because \(0.7\times1.3=0.91\) either way.
  • Adding and subtracting percentages directly. Percentages of different bases do not add.

Why A is right Taking the original as 100, the reduced price is 70. Increasing 70 by 30 percent adds \(0.3\times 70=21\), giving 91. The final price is 91 percent of the original.

Why B is wrong The two changes cancel only if both percentages are taken of the same base. The decrease is 30 percent of 100 and the increase is 30 percent of 70, so they are different amounts.

Why C is wrong 109 comes from adding 30 percent of the original to the original and then subtracting a smaller amount, which reverses the order of the two changes and still uses the wrong base.

Why D is wrong 60 treats the two changes as a single 40 percent reduction, or subtracts 30 from 100 twice minus 10. No sequence of the given changes produces it.

skill: Ratios, rates, proportional relationships, and units
stem_html: A printing press produces 45 pages every 20 seconds. At this rate, how many minutes does it take to produce 8,100 pages?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The unit is italicised for a reason. The natural computation lands in seconds.
  • Counting intervals. \(8100/45\) is a count of 20-second blocks, not a time.
  • Which way up the rate goes. Pages per second and seconds per page are reciprocals.

Why A is right The rate is \(\dfrac{45}{20}=2.25\) pages per second, so 8,100 pages take \(\dfrac{8100}{2.25}=3600\) seconds, which is \(\dfrac{3600}{60}=60\) minutes.

Why B is wrong 3,600 is the answer in seconds. The question asks for minutes, and the final division by 60 is the step most often skipped.

Why C is wrong 180 is \(8100/45\), the number of 20-second intervals, treated as though each interval were a minute.

Why D is wrong 30 inverts the rate somewhere in the chain, using \(20/45\) as pages per second rather than seconds per page.

skill: One-variable data: Distributions and measures of center and spread
stem_html: A data set of 9 values has a mean of 12 and a median of 10. The largest value, 30, is replaced by 48. What are the mean and median of the new data set?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "The mean is 14 and the median is 10."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "The mean is 12 and the median is 10.", "trap": "mean-vs-median"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "The mean is 14 and the median is 12.", "trap": "mean-vs-median"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "The mean is 30 and the median is 10.", "trap": "solved-wrong-quantity"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • One statistic moves and the other does not. Two choices change both or neither.
  • Sum first. Working from \(n\times\) mean is faster than trying to reconstruct the values.
  • The median's position. With 9 values it is the fifth, and the change happens at the ninth.

Why A is right The sum was \(9\times 12=108\); replacing 30 with 48 adds 18, giving 126, so the new mean is \(\dfrac{126}{9}=14\). The median is the fifth value in order, and increasing the largest value cannot move it, so the median stays 10.

Why B is wrong The mean does change. Every value contributes to the mean, so raising one of them by 18 raises the total by 18.

Why C is wrong The median does not change. The fifth-largest value is unaffected by what happens above it, which is exactly why the median is described as resistant.

Why D is wrong 30 is the value that was removed. Neither the mean nor the median of the new set is a value from the old one.

stem_html: Of 200 students surveyed, 120 take Spanish, 90 take French, and 40 take both. If a student who takes French is selected at random, what is the probability that the student also takes Spanish?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The denominator is the condition. “Given French” makes 90 the total.
  • The two conditionals are not equal. 40 out of 90 and 40 out of 120 answer opposite questions.
  • The unconditional probability is a decoy and is the easiest fraction to form.

Why A is right The condition restricts the sample space to the 90 French students, and 40 of them take Spanish, so the probability is \(\dfrac{40}{90}=\dfrac{4}{9}\).

Why B is wrong \(\dfrac{40}{120}\) conditions on Spanish instead of French. That is the probability a Spanish student takes French, which is a different question.

Why C is wrong \(\dfrac{40}{200}\) uses the whole survey as the denominator, which answers “what fraction of all students take both” and ignores the condition.

Why D is wrong \(\dfrac{80}{200}\) or \(\dfrac{2}{5}\) is not a probability the table supports; it comes from doubling the overlap or from mixing the two conditional denominators.

stem_html: A line of best fit for a scatterplot of \(y\) against \(x\) is \(\hat{y}=3.4x+18\). One data point has \(x=10\) and \(y=46\). What is the residual for this point?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Order of subtraction. Observed minus predicted, always.
  • The sign is the content. A negative residual says the point sits below the line.
  • Two of the choices are numbers already computed on the way, which makes them feel like results.

Why A is right The predicted value is \(3.4(10)+18=52\), and the residual is observed minus predicted: \(46-52=-6\).

Why B is wrong 6 is predicted minus observed. The residual is defined the other way round, and its sign carries the information that the point lies below the line.

Why C is wrong 52 is the predicted value, the output of the model rather than the gap between the model and the data.

Why D is wrong 46 is the observed value, which the question supplies.

stem_html: After a 15 percent increase, the number of members of a club is 322. How many members were there before the increase?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Undoing a percentage increase is a division. Subtracting the same percentage from the new value overshoots, because the base has changed.
  • Direction of the change. The answer must be smaller than 322.
  • Percent against count. 15 is not a number of members.

Why A is right If \(m\) is the original count then \(1.15m=322\), so \(m=\dfrac{322}{1.15}=280\). Checking, \(280\times 1.15=322\).

Why B is wrong 274 is \(322\) reduced by 15 percent: \(322\times 0.85=273.7\). Reversing an increase means dividing by 1.15, not subtracting 15 percent of the new total.

Why C is wrong 370 increases 322 by 15 percent instead of undoing the increase.

Why D is wrong 307 subtracts 15 from 322, treating the percentage as a count of members.

skill: One-variable data: Distributions and measures of center and spread
stem_html: Two classes took the same test. Class A has 10 students with a mean score of 78. Class B has 30 students with a mean score of 86. What is the mean score of all 40 students?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Averaging the averages. It is right only for equal group sizes.
  • The answer must lie between 78 and 86, and closer to 86 than to 78.
  • Weight by count, not by number of groups.

Why A is right The totals are \(10\times 78=780\) and \(30\times 86=2580\), so the combined total is 3,360 and the mean is \(\dfrac{3360}{40}=84\).

Why B is wrong 82 is the average of 78 and 86, which would be right only if the two classes were the same size. Class B is three times as large and pulls the mean toward 86.

Why C is wrong 83 is the midpoint nudged one point toward the larger class, a common way of guessing at a weighted mean without computing it.

Why D is wrong 86 is Class B's mean. It is the value the combined mean approaches as Class B grows, but Class A's ten students keep it below 86.

stem_html: In the \(xy\)-plane, the equation of a circle is \(x^{2}+y^{2}-6x+10y+18=0\). What is the radius of the circle?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Stopping at \(r^{2}\). The standard form gives the square.
  • Two constants get subtracted, not one. Completing the square in both variables moves 9 and 25 across.
  • The halved coefficients locate the centre, and neither of them is a radius.

Why A is right Completing the square gives \((x-3)^{2}-9+(y+5)^{2}-25+18=0\), so \((x-3)^{2}+(y+5)^{2}=16\) and the radius is \(\sqrt{16}=4\).

Why B is wrong 16 is \(r^{2}\). The equation in standard form ends at the square of the radius, and one square root remains.

Why C is wrong \(\sqrt{18}\) reads the constant term 18 as \(r^{2}\) without completing the square. The 18 is what is left over before the two completed squares are subtracted.

Why D is wrong 2 comes from halving \(-6\) and taking that as the radius; \(-6/2=-3\) is the \(x\)-coordinate of the centre, not a length.

stem_html: In right triangle \(ABC\), angle \(C\) is the right angle, \(AC=9\) and \(BC=12\). What is the value of \(\sin A\)?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Which leg is opposite \(A\). The side opposite an angle is the one that does not touch it, and \(BC\) is that side.
  • Every ratio of 9, 12 and 15 is offered. Naming the function is the whole problem.
  • The hypotenuse has to be computed first, and neither leg is it.

Why A is right The hypotenuse is \(AB=\sqrt{9^{2}+12^{2}}=15\). The side opposite angle \(A\) is \(BC=12\), so \(\sin A=\dfrac{12}{15}=\dfrac{4}{5}\).

Why B is wrong \(\dfrac{9}{15}\) uses \(AC\), the side adjacent to angle \(A\). That is \(\cos A\).

Why C is wrong \(\dfrac{12}{9}\) is opposite over adjacent, which is \(\tan A\). Sine takes the hypotenuse as its denominator.

Why D is wrong \(\dfrac{9}{12}\) is adjacent over opposite, the reciprocal of the tangent.

stem_html: A right circular cylinder has radius \(r\) and height \(h\). A second cylinder has radius \(2r\) and height \(\dfrac{h}{2}\). The volume of the second cylinder is how many times the volume of the first?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Only one dimension is squared. Doubling \(r\) multiplies the volume by 4.
  • The cancelling instinct. A doubling and a halving look like they undo each other.
  • Both changes matter, and two choices use only one of them.

Why A is right The volume is \(\pi r^{2}h\). The second is \(\pi(2r)^{2}\left(\dfrac{h}{2}\right)=\pi\cdot 4r^{2}\cdot\dfrac{h}{2}=2\pi r^{2}h\), which is twice the first.

Why B is wrong 1 assumes doubling the radius and halving the height cancel. They do not: the radius is squared and the height is not.

Why C is wrong 4 applies the squared factor from the radius and forgets the height entirely.

Why D is wrong \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) applies the height factor and forgets the radius.

stem_html: In triangle \(PQR\), the measure of angle \(P\) is \(3x^{\circ}\), the measure of angle \(Q\) is \((x+20)^{\circ}\), and the measure of angle \(R\) is \((2x-8)^{\circ}\). What is the measure, in degrees, of the largest angle?
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Solving for \(x\) and stopping. \(x\) is among the choices.
  • Two of the three angles are equal, so the largest is not the one most students compute first.
  • Dropping a constant when substituting. \(2x-8\) is not \(2x\).

Why A is right The angles sum to 180, so \(3x+x+20+2x-8=180\), \(6x+12=180\) and \(x=28\). The angles are \(84^{\circ}\), \(48^{\circ}\) and \(48^{\circ}\), so the largest is 84.

Why B is wrong 48 is the measure of the other two angles, which are equal. The question asks for the largest.

Why C is wrong 28 is the value of \(x\). It is the last number computed before the question is answered.

Why D is wrong 56 is \(2x\), which is the measure of angle \(R\) with the \(-8\) dropped.
